241.s: After first jobs he finds Moneta, a teacher he knew from home, and takes lessons for two or three years; he fetches his book.
241.q: Yeah, yeah, yeah. So, so he said, so we wouldn't, we wouldn't take no job. We just rehearsal. So after we, the first job we got, we played for some, oh, Beville Garden, on Beville Street. It rained all day and all night. And then the first job we played for White. That's in, uh, in the Algae area.…

241.s: Charlie DeVoy says Thomas studied the Arban method; Thomas recalls the thick, hard book.
241.q: No. I got a book man but that was thick man.

241.t: Growing up in Napoleonville and learning trombone
241.s: Nelson was raised in Napoleonville, studied trombone with Professor Williams and admired Lawrence Johnson.
241.q: No, I left New Orleans when I was about two months old. Went to a place out in the country named Napoleonville. I spent about 25 years out there.

297.t: Taking up trombone in 1925 and his teachers
297.s: He took up trombone in 1925 and studied with Vic Gaspard, Sonny Henry and others, naming Harrison Bradley and more.
297.q: With Vic Gaspar. Mm-hmm. And Sonny Henry gave me a few lessons too. You did hear? Sonny Henry. Yeah. And Yank Johnson. Who was that? I've heard of him.

297.t: Trombone lessons with Vic Gaspard and Sonny Henry
297.s: He studied trombone with Vic Gaspard (longest) and Sonny Henry; a garbled stretch of the tape follows.
297.q: Yeah. Where did you buy a trombone and how old were you? Yeah. Yeah. Where did you buy a trombone and how old were you? Yeah.

297.t: Gaspard as strict musician, and lesson prices
297.s: Gaspard taught by music, not jazz; he charged Summers a dollar and a quarter for about two hours.
297.ch: Vic Gaspard and the Lyric Theatre
297.q: No, no, he's strictly a musician. He didn't play no, no Dixieland much. Yeah. He didn't play by air. He didn't play by air. Uh-huh. Play it all by everything? He'd buy music, everything by music. Well, what, did he teach you to play by music? He teach me to play by music, but he used to play by…

825.t: Metoyer's slow start: sixteen lessons before touching the horn
825.s: Metoyer first taught reading, then had his daughter play major and minor chords for Ernie to identify, and made him learn the parts of the horn. Ernie could not play with others for a year or two.
825.q: Well I stayed with Alma Twi for about two years. You started right at the beginning? And then he died. Have you been blowing on the horn at all? No, right from the beginning. But it was about, I took about sixteen lessons before he'd ever let me touch the horn. Just reading music? Just reading…

825.s: Ernie describes Metoyer's patient teaching and the books he used: a French method first, then the Arban method.
825.q: Well, I'll tell you one thing he was. Yes, he was very determined in teaching here. And he had very much patience. He would give you a lesson and...

825.t: Lesson schedule and the fifty-cent fee
825.s: Lessons were twice a week for an hour at fifty cents. After the fourteenth lesson Metoyer waived the fee whenever Ernie knew his lesson.
825.q: Fifty cents a lesson. And after my fourteenth lesson, he promised me that every lesson that I would bring back to him, and if I knew it, I wouldn't have to pay him. For his. That's right. And he would always give my lesson, and from then on I ain't given fifty cents yet. I was fighting him. He was…

240.t: How Shalini taught, and fellow student Lionel Ferbos
240.s: He cannot say how Shalini taught. He recalls going to lessons with Lionel Ferbos, who had asthma, and getting ahead of the music on his horn.
240.q: I don't exactly know if he did. But most of all, I know who was going over there. Do you know Lionel Ferbis? No. Lionel Ferbis, he said no.

240.t: Lessons with Manuel Perez from the Auburn book
240.s: He had few lessons with Perez, who left for Chicago and sent him to Sidney Desvigne.
240.q: Yes, he did from the Auburn book. But I didn't take too many lessons from him because he left and went to Chicago. Then, so he suggested that I go to Sidney Desveen, had been his pupil previously, maybe, oh I don't know, maybe 10, 12, 15 years previously he had been by his pupil. And in turn he…

177.t: Professor Chaligny's lessons and big student band
177.s: Uncle Clay took him to Old Man Chaligny, who taught at his St. Claude Street home for 25 cents and ran a large scholars' band that rehearsed at a hall.
177.q: Well I got the set and my Uncle Clay taking me to Old Man Chaloner for lessons. And Old Man Chaloner was a teacher. He didn't only teach you. He made you experience of learning to play instruments. He would have a big band of all of his scholars. On Monday you'd go to lessons. On Wednesday all his…

177.t: Lessons and the school band of Old Man Chaligny
177.s: Chaligny ran a school band and taught many students, including Jiles, Kid Howard and his future father-in-law.
177.q: Well that was mostly a band that he had a school and when he got occasionally, got jobs, well he used them. But practically he teaching all the fellows, you see. Because that's who I went to lesson on there, Old Man Chalini. He was a great teacher. He would have 40 men and if he wanted to make a…

35.t: Visiting Bunk for lessons and the Calypso melody
35.s: Blumberg went to Bunk's afternoons to find his secrets, and Bunk played a Calypso tune he had picked up in Harlem.
35.q: Yeah, I remember the concert, and I remember being kind of disappointed, and you know, the funk just felt so bad, and so forth. But anyway, those were the lessons. I mean, he invited me up to spend the afternoons with him and take lessons or what have you, you know. And I'd come up to wherever he…

35.t: The Imperial Method and what Bunk marked for practice
35.s: Bunk charged nothing and told Blumberg to get the Imperial Method; he marked lines, advised octaves and foot beat.
35.q: Oh, no, he never, he never charged. He never charged. He told me to get this book. I guess he said either get Arbenz or the Imperial Method. And so I got the Imperial Method.

185.t: Father and uncle as teachers, Sousa band and arranging
185.s: Father and uncle insisted on years of solfege, taught pupils like George Baquet and Achille Baquet, and the uncle played with Sousa and earned money transposing and arranging.
185.q: That's right. Provided with hearing. Hearing. You see, they were great teachers. That's one thing they were. They were great teachers. They turned out many, many, many scholars. They turned out, such as George A. Paquet. He was a famous guy. He was taught by my uncle. And, um, there's, uh, Asheel…

185.t: How the Tios gave lessons: method, group duets, fees and schedules
185.s: Lorenzo and Uncle Papa left pupils to practice and returned to correct them, refused money from pupils with no hearing, taught duets, charged 75 cents or a dollar, and pupils came once or twice a week.
185.q: That's right. He'd tell you you didn't want your money. Right. I remember right down the valley street, a fellow came to him and he said to him and he took several lessons with me. And he told the boy, he said, let me tell you something. I want to talk to your daddy. He did. He went and spoke to…

257.t: Trombone teachers: Gene Ware, Pinchback Tureaud, Eddie Pearson
257.s: His first trombone teacher was Gene Ware, followed by lessons with Pinchback Tureaud and Eddie Pearson while still playing drums in the school band.
257.q: Oh definitely, definitely, see, because in the meantime I was learning, I was going, my first teacher on trombone was Gene Ware, because I used to rehearse at the house with my brother, see.

257.s: They try to pin down the name of his first method book, 'White Excelsior', and he mentions starting on valve trombone.
257.q: Yeah, I, it was, let's see, the first method. Matter of fact, I started my little ball off with one. It was white, let me see, white, white flamm or white something, I forgot to, I knew it was white something method.

619.t: Method books and continued lessons with several teachers
619.s: He used the Klose method and others, and kept taking lessons with his sister, Lorenzo Tio, Papa Tio and another teacher.
619.ch: Clarinet fingering and the Tio family
619.q: I just used them. I gave a couple of them away. I used a closed-air and I used a fool with this method. You see, that's where I was living. stuff with stuff with

619.t: Papa Tio's strict lessons, fees and teaching method
619.s: Papa Tio sent pupils home if they had not learned the lesson, charged Laurent fifty cents against two dollars from white pupils, and taught counting and solfege.
619.ch: Lessons with Papa Tio and Helen Edwards
619.q: Well, Papa Teo was very good. He taught, he taught you all kinds of, uh, Peiju was, uh, he taught you how to master your cards. He taught you, you, different keys that you could pick up, a number so easy. You'd pick up a number so easy. He'd teach you the cards that you could pick up easily. You…

46.t: Preston Jackson, Oscar Young's band at the Red Mill and lessons
46.s: He sat under Preston Jackson at the Red Mill dances, begged lessons, moved next door to him, and was passed on to Roy Palmer.
46.ch: Teachers: Preston Jackson and Roy Palmer
46.q: Well, who has done more for me than anyone? Well, as I said, I was with Jackson for a few years, and he gave me all the fundamentals of things. But Preston Jackson was with the band. There was a place at 43rd and State Street upstairs. It was called the Red Mill. And, of course, I was on...it was…

46.t: Never oiling the slide and the woman teacher
46.s: A woman teacher at the school finds his slide corroded because he never oiled it; he explains why he preferred her to Jackson.
46.q: And he had a lady there that was a teacher, she was a teacher and instructor in the school. So one day I happened to get her to give me my lessons, see. So she taking my horn to show me a passage, you know, how it should be played.

1008.t: Lessons with Chaligny: method, price and fellow players
1008.s: Lessons used the Otto method at fifty cents, twice a week; Earl Fouche taught him tenor ideas.
1008.ch: Lessons, WPA band and sidemen years
1008.q: Well, yeah, we used to use, uh, an auto language at that time, you see. And I'd taken lessons with him through the auto language on a clarinet.

1008.t: Chaligny's pupils and the advertising brass band
1008.s: Brother Cornbread studied with old man Chaligny, whose pupil brass band advertised dances from a truck.
1008.ch: Lessons, WPA band and sidemen years
1008.q: Well, Brother Cornbread used to take lessons with old man Chalney. Him and I was a scholar over there, because he had a very large place, and he had just so many youngsters.

828.t: Humphrey's lessons and his club orchestra
828.s: Details of the lessons: twice a week, 50 cents, at Humphrey's home, and the club orchestra rehearsing at members' houses.
828.q: He had an orchestra. And the orchestra had... Used to go around to different ones' houses and they'd practice each week.

828.t: Leaving Humphrey for Chalamet; Humphrey's instruments
828.s: He studied with Humphrey until about 1922, then took private lessons from Chalamet in the military band; Humphrey's main instrument was trumpet but he played others.
828.q: Now, I went to him, that was around, I was 19, 20. And I stayed with him until around 21, or the first part, middle part of 22 or something like that. Well then, I got in this military band and they had a man, Professor Chalamet, I heard of him. See? Well after, so I stopped taking lessons with…

475.t: Dave Perkins's death and Sunday band lessons
475.s: French recalls Perkins dying around 1940, nearly 100, and his Sunday band lessons around 1931-32 at Central Road.
475.q: I don't have the date on Dave Perkins. I think Dave Perkins died, I don't know, I think maybe around the 40s. I'm not sure. Somewhere around the 40s, 39 or 40.

475.t: Lessons with Jim Humphrey and Willie Foster
475.s: French took a few lessons from Professor Jim Humphrey and from Willie Foster, with Russell on Foster's health and age.
475.q: Yeah. The older musicians anyhow, they all took lessons from Dave Perkins. And well, then some of them I mean I did went to Professor Humphrey a while but I didn't go there too long. Well I've heard of Jim Humphrey, that's the grandfather of Percy and all that. Yeah that's right, well I didn't go…

798.t: Perkins' character, strict lessons and his lamp-lit back-room studio
798.s: Perkins was light-skinned, friendly but strict, demonstrated on each instrument, and taught in a back room by oil lamp.
798.q: Oh yeah, he was strict. If you went there, you see when you take a lesson and, uh, when you get through, you say, well we'll try this next week. He'll turn that page. He'll run two, three lines with you, say that'll be enough for you to practice. And he'll stay on that with you 10 or 15 minutes and…

798.t: Lesson price, Perkins' memories of Clark's father Aaron, counting with the foot
798.s: A dollar an hour lesson; Perkins liked to talk about Clark's father Aaron and the Onward and Excelsior bands; he taught counting by foot.
798.q: When you sit down and he looked at his watch and he didn't stop and lose no other time when you're talking. He kept you on that instrument. Now when your time was up he'd pull his watch up and say, well your time is up but let me run over this with you.

106.t: Edmund Jenkins urges more study; the $5 lesson with Dumont
106.s: Jenkins in London suggested he continue studying; Briggs recalls his single paid lessons with the Hippodrome trumpeter Dumont and comments on what lessons cost.
106.ch: New York, church bands and early training
106.q: You see, they had background, they knew what they were doing. Today, if you can't arrange, if you don't know your keys, all your keys, you can't be a professor, you can't teach. You have to know everything in order to teach pupils. And that the majority didn't have. And I was fortunate when I went…

106.t: Lessons with John Solomon in London
106.s: Jenkins introduced him to John Solomon, a leading London teacher, with whom he studied for a couple of years and gained full control of the instrument.
106.ch: New York, church bands and early training
106.q: But I just -- I'd taken two lessons from him, but I appreciated everything he did, 'cause everything -- I realized when Mr. Jenkins introduced me to Mr. John Simon Solomon who was the solo trumpetist at the London Symphony, and a Principal teacher at the Royal Academy, which is now the London…

174.t: First lessons with Professor Nickerson and Frank Crump
174.s: His first note-reading lessons were with Professor Nickerson; Frank Crump taught him at home while his regular teacher was away. They discuss which Nickerson he studied with.
174.q: No, because the first thing I ever, the first note music I ever took was with Professor Nickerson. And I never mentioned this to you, a Crump, a Frank Crump, when T.O. was away a while, before I went with Shalini a while, well he used to come at my house and give me music lessons, his name is Frank…

242.t: Quitting the horn after his grandfather's death; Professor Milton and learning by ear
242.s: He put the trumpet away after his grandfather died, found it dusty, took lessons from Professor Milton but got by copying records and playing by ear.
242.q: You know? When did you first learn to read that? Well, now, that came years and years later. That's right. When I first learned, learned to read. Well, all right. That went on there. So, but then I don't know, something happened and I stopped fooling with the trumpet. See? I remember that distinct.…

929.t: Lessons that are just talking; musicians DeVore learned from
929.s: DeVore says lessons can be talk about life, and names Kid Punch, Kid Thomas, Manuel Perez and Johnny Wiggs as the trumpet men he spent most time with.
929.ch: Band building and learning from musicians
929.q: Yeah, sure. I don't see why not. That's the idea I had. And a lot of times the lessons wouldn't be involved with playing the instrument at all. Just talking. Talking to them. Understanding maybe the kind of life they led. This all goes into New Orleans music. Who did you go and talk to? Well, the…

245.t: Favorite trumpeter Perez, lessons with Humphrey and the Arban method
245.s: Perez was his favorite but sent him to Humphrey. He studied the Arban method and later got ideas from Fess Manetta.
245.q: Did you like better than anybody else? Yeah, I certainly did. My favorite trumpet player was Manuel Perez. I went to him to get some lessons, you know, take lessons from him. Well he had his hand full. You see, he couldn't take me, but he recommended Professor Humphrey. That's how I started taking…

709.t: Chris Kelly takes up trumpet; star pupil of Professor Humphrey
709.s: Chris took up trumpet in his late teens or early twenties, learned quickly, and was an excellent reader. He studied with Professor Humphrey, whose son Willie the clarinetist is mentioned, and played in both brass and string bands.
709.q: He was a number one reader. He was. Really good. He was really good. You could get any piece of music you could put up there. He would look at it and cast his eye down on it. That was all right. He got it, son. Yeah. Yeah. But give him that. Who was him? Heisenborns, Peter Anderson, and well, see…

178.t: Cornet to trumpet and later teachers
178.s: He began on cornet, moved to trumpet, took lessons about two years with Shawnee then Manuel Perez and others, learning theory and reading.
178.q: Oh, I think, living with Shawnee, about a couple years, and then I took lessons with, uh, uh, Uh, Narmie Pond. Snire, Manny Perez, Uh-huh. and later on with, uh, several castigots.

689.t: Opening and Manuel Perez as a patient, sight-reading teacher
689.s: Dominique gives his name, then describes teacher Manuel Perez: strict about lessons, an accomplished reader who sight-read at the Deluxe Cafe.
689.ch: New Orleans teachers and classical musicians
689.q: I can tell you a lot about him, Bill. Manuel Perez was a very patient man giving lessons. And he's a very accomplished musician, a good musician. One man, if you didn't know all of your lessons, you missed one measure, he'd send you back home and give you the same lesson, or he wouldn't stand for…

955.t: Trumpet teachers and Manuel Perez as a player
955.s: He studied trumpet with Chaligny, Manuel Perez and a rough teacher; he describes Perez as a straight, strong brass-band leader who never varied.
955.q: Well no I went under Chalini when I'd taken up trumpet. I stayed with Chalini about six months and I left him and I went with Manuel Perez. I went with Ole Man Adolf Alexander which we called North Byrne by the name of Taton. I stayed with him about three or four weeks. He was kind of rough. I had…

183.t: Strict teachers: no touching the instrument until the notes are learned
183.s: Alfred and Watts compare teachers who held back the instrument for two years; Watts's father bought him the Otto Langey method book before the horn.
183.ch: Learning trumpet and first bands in New Orleans
183.q: Yeah. Well, that's it. You see. And he wanted them different keys. He wanted me to know what I'm going to do when I'm running up on a flat or a sharp or a double flat or a double sharp. He wanted to know just what I'm going to, what I would do. See. In front of the book, they had their fing ring.…

255.s: He studied with Professor David Jones, who retaught everything from method books at 50 cents a lesson twice a week.
255.q: Did you take any lessons or did you just learn at home? Well, I started playing from around with some of the upper grade musicians. Then I went to Professor David Jones, but they don't accept what somebody else teach you. But then he took me back over everything that they had learnt me to review…

771.s: He learned trumpet fingering in a couple of lessons from Brookhoven, and taught himself trombone and xylophone.
771.q: Well the old man Brookhoven, he had a band, he was an old German, you know. And the Brookhoven band, Brass Band, you know. He had a couple of boys play trumpet and one played in the theater, you know. Leo I think his name was, but his daddy, well you see I was a musician already because I was…

872.t: Tio's lessons: duets and figuring out music
872.s: Gorman recounts Tio's duets with pupils and his view of working out music like counting money.
872.q: Well, I tell you what you do. As long as you was going along, all right, he let you go. You understand what I mean? Now, now and then him and I used to make duets together. He said, well, all right, you're doing fine. Now let's take this duet tonight. He said, now what line you want to take? The…

624.t: Lessons, Grover's band and playing at Tom Anderson's
624.s: Brunies mentions a few lessons from Johnny DeDroit and an old trombonist, then the band with Grover, his wife and others at Tom Anderson's place near Canal and Rampart, where he stayed while Armstrong went north.
624.q: Did you ever play with them? No. Johnny played Trump. Johnny played Trump. Johnny played Trump. I took a couple lessons from Johnny, but I didn't like it. I figured it would come out of my head. He was better than sitting down with music. Yeah. Yeah. He's one of our old neighbors, Johnny Deetra.…

258.t: Learning trombone from Maurice French and Bill Matthews
258.s: He bought a trombone in Alexandria, had lessons from Maurice French, played solos on the job, and later studied with Bill Matthews.
258.ch: Learning drums and trombone, New Orleans
258.q: And so I put it down. And after putting the clarinet down, I was still thinking of a double, so I got it on the trombone.

568.t: Learning from Roy Palmer and the visit from teacher Dave Perkins
568.s: Roy shows him how to blow the horn and proposes a band; trombonist Dave Perkins hears him practising and warns him to learn music.
568.q: Roy brought me a horn. I shined the horn up, cleaned the horn. About an hour after I cleaned the horn and was sitting down in the back. There wasn't much during that night and my knee wasn't there. I didn't use him until late at night anyway. Roy come in. And I said, yeah, man, I'm pulling with…

662.s: She credits Mrs. Anna Stewart, a New England Conservatory graduate, with her foundation in harmony, theory and thoroughbass.
662.q: I had various teachers, but the one to whom I give all credit was a Mrs. Stewart, because she gave me a foundation and a basic that one gets in college now. Transposition and Thoroughbass and Harmony, Theory, and all of that I had under her. And you don't get that until you advance, but she gave me…

251.s: His stolen Clodomir method and solfege books, and what music is.
251.q: It was called the Clodermier. C-L-O-U-D-M-I-E-R. It's the old French method. And it had everything in it. It had, from the beginning, the whole notes, then the half notes, then the quarter notes, and so forth and so on. And there were a lot of solos in there that were taken from Poet and Peasant…

1057.t: Piano teachers Camilla Todd and Massey DeVoyne; learning to read
1057.s: He studied with Camilla Todd, a church pianist who also played dance music, and with Miss Massey DeVoyne. He already played by ear and was taught to read.
1057.q: And she used to play in the church at the First Street Baptist Church. That's the First Street Drive. Oh, that's the first town. Yeah. And I take lessons under her and I take lessons under another lady by name was Miss DeVoyne. Massey DeVoyne. I've heard her name. She used to live on Pusha Street.…

903.t: Lessons from Jim Humphrey and learning from Armstrong records
903.s: Clayton took lessons from Jim Humphrey with a method book, then learned tunes like Muskrat Ramble from Louis Armstrong records and turned down a road offer.
903.q: and he said, yeah well, we took lessons from him and after he'd taken sick, well he didn't give them no more, we'd get around there and do it ourself, you see.

11.t: Lessons with Papa Tio: method book, fees and manner
11.s: What Tio taught, the method book, 25 cents a lesson, and his own earlier schooling in notes.
11.q: made you do when you went there on the for a lesson oh yeah I bought a method the method cost a dollar quarter at that time and I'm trying to think of the name of it now if I can and you start in the beginning of the book where you have your whole notes quarter notes and as you advance and you have…

14.t: Teaching himself from piano books and practicing with Harry
14.s: Love tells how he studied Cecilia's piano books in a wash shed as a boy and later practiced the Red Book every day with clarinetist Harry in Alexandria.
14.q: I catch one band maybe play one or two of them, and the other band maybe play two or three of them. I used to study them books. Cecilia kind of had books like that, but just for piano, you know. And boy she could play some piano. She learned that in England. And she finished college over there. She…

448.t: First lessons: price, setup and Bechet's enthusiasm
448.s: Wilber was the school's only student at $5 a lesson; Bechet was keen to teach his idea of improvisation.
448.q: And so I, I came over and, and, uh, bought my clarinet and played for him. And I guess he, he was really pleased at the start because I obviously was trying to play like he, you know, he was my idol.

271.t: Leonce's instruments and trombone playing; teachers
271.s: Leonce moved from mandolin to guitar, string bass and trombone; Mello praises him and names other trombonists he played with, then mentions Father Reuther at Holy Cross as a teacher.
271.ch: Early string bands and first jobs
271.q: No, his head, he had the brains and he had the ear. I see. He had the head, the brains, and the ear. What did you say he first started playing? Manning. And then he switched to... To guitar. And then he played what? Bass, string bass. And then? Trombone. Sliphorn. Sliphorn.

187.t: Lessons from Williams: fees, strictness and counting with the foot
187.s: Lessons cost fifty cents; Williams was strict and taught counting by foot-tapping.
187.q: At his home, and he used to come down, all, if he got a, let's say like if he got a student in Bellrose, he'd come down there that day. If he got one in Pankoville, come down to Pointville to teach me, he made all he had that particular day to come, see? And then go back, but most of his teaching…

12.t: Lessons with Papa Tio and the 1939 return to New Orleans
12.s: Tio made him learn notes before playing; in 1939 he saw old-timers who had other trades while touring with Russell.
12.q: Did you? Well, I had to. No, no. Yeah. Papa, he gave me lessons a few months before he let me play the horn. He wanted me to get the rudiments of the music. Because he said, you've got plenty of time to learn this jazz. He used to call it ragtime then. There was no such thing as jazz when I was…

279.t: Lessons with Vic Lebowski and the legitimate pianists
279.s: Hug studied with technician Vic Lebowski and discusses other legitimate pianists.
279.q: Do I remember Vic Lebowski? Oh, I took lessons from Vic. After I left Mrs. Asap, as I told you, I began just going out on my own, you know, and learning the jazz tunes and learning how to play jazz. But then after a couple of years I realized that I should improve a little bit on my technique and…

875.t: Teachers: Professor Delmar, Chris Kelly and Paul Barnes
875.s: Howard studied with Professor Delmar and Chris; learned reading and arranging from Paul Barnes at La Vida.
875.q: Oh Professor Delmar, he was a professor, but I'd taken lessons quite a while with him. In fact most of the fellas did at that time. Where did he live? Well he had lived in a city but he was from some part of the country I just remember.

724.t: Papa Tio and Lorenzo Tio as teachers; lessons from Big Eye Louis
724.s: The interviewers talk about Papa Tio's pupils; Burbank took a few lessons from Big Eye Louis Nelson.
724.q: It was before your time, right? That was before my time, yeah. And had I, well, I don't remember when did he die, but I don't believe he was dead yet, you know, when I was trying to get somebody to teach me if I could do anything about him. Probably I'd have been able to get him.

713.t: Learning from his uncle, his brother and Milano
713.s: His uncle and brother gave him tips; he studied about six months with Milano, who had no method book and showed chords on his horn, and Nelson played by ear.
713.q: used with you or what he did well it is showman is telling me to make the cause and this you know you take his horn and show me from his own yeah I finally don't get though did you have a regular

189.t: Teaching Earl Palmer, Frank Mitchell, Milton Batiste and Melvin Lastie
189.s: Students including Earl Palmer and Frank Mitchell, who became his student; Willie Humphrey, Milton Batiste.
189.q: Yeah. Well Earl was in my harmony class and he was in my sight singing class. And I would teach them how to read rhythms. And he was very good at it. But I was the only one at the school who was teaching rhythms. You know like they would teach the rhythm along with the melody. But they depend upon…

190.t: Professor theory book, hot toddy advice and Dejan's trumpet lesson
190.s: They recall a teacher's handwritten theory book and his quarter lessons; Dejan tells of his hot-water-and-whiskey advice and being made to play at his brother's lesson.
190.q: That's right. That's right. That's right. That's right. That's right. Sing everything you play, sing it. Yeah, that's right. Yeah. Yeah.

778.t: Teacher Florida Beck, Professor Bennett, and no lessons for her sisters
778.s: Her unreliable teacher Florida Beck, Professor Bennett, her good ear, and later study in New York.
778.q: How about Florida Beck? Florida Beck, she taught me music there in Pensacola. Oh she did? But the father, you get so high, I couldn't be bothered by the father. Yeah. If Florida get high, she wouldn't show up. Yeah. I told my mother, I said, you're paying all that money money for me. I said,…

48.t: Trombone method books and how he began
48.s: Method books he used, solfege questions, and a teacher saying he was a natural.
48.q: Yeah, I can't think of the name. Now, let's see. His name is a book now. I'll give this boy one. He's good. A trumpet? Yeah. I can't think of that mouthpiece. That book.

841.t: Lessons with Professor Raleigh and Davy Jones, and teaching methods
841.s: Harris's father gave no lessons; he studied with Raleigh and then Davy Jones, and compares old and current method books.
841.q: or did how did you learn my father never did lesson you see I'll tell you I'll tell you what my father didn't help me my mother didn't land the holly and you see where the music he didn't want nothing to see that's not practice he'd get on out the house and go I had a good teacher professor Raleigh…

288.t: Lessons in 1909 from Moret; two Moret brothers
288.s: Charles went to New Orleans to study in 1909 with Moret on Ursuline Street; he separates Eugene (white bands) from George (Excelsior).
288.ch: Vidals, blues, teachers and the Silver Leaf band
288.q: When I first went to New Orleans I went to study music. That was your first time? Oh yeah. That was my first time in New Orleans. In 1909 I went to study music. And I was taking lessons from Mr. Moret on Ursuline Street. Which one? Eugene. That's the one who used to play with only white bands.…

879.t: Teacher Waddell Corzell and first parade with Anderson Minor
879.s: He studied under Corzell at Crescent City Music School; Minor Anderson gave him pointers at his first carnival parade.
879.q: No, I took, uh, this is when I really started. I took, uh, music lessons underneath the direction of, uh, Mr. Waddell Corzell. He taught me the valve trombone. It was, uh, sort of simple. And, when I switched over to the slide trombone, he was still my, uh, music teacher every Saturday. It was, uh,…

176.t: De De's teacher Charlot and his influences
176.s: He learned his notes from Charlot, a letter carrier, was influenced by Rene and Chris Kelly, and picked up mute playing himself.
176.q: And when he wasn't busy he was resting at home. I left my wife and tell me, you know, one of those things, you know, resting or so. So I left him and I went to a fellow we called Charlotte and he was a letter carrier, he was an old man. St. Claude, I think he was in the main. He used to teach, you…

193.t: Lessons with Paul Chaligny and Kid Rena
193.s: He studied about a year with letter carrier Paul Chaligny, then took lessons from Kid Rena, whose style he liked.
193.q: Well, I like Rene. Kid Rene playing. I went to Rene for a while afterwards, you know? Oh, I see. He taught you some lessons, too. Yeah, I taught you some lessons, too.

127.t: Joe Howard, the trumpeter who taught Punch
127.s: Punch says Joe Howard showed him a lot on trumpet before he left New Orleans, and learns Howard has died.
127.q: Joe Howard used to be a trumpet player, but tell me he got on bass. But I can say this. Before I left here, Joe Howard showed me a whole lot of stuff on trumpet. And gave me a whole lot of musical ideas. He was a mighty fine man, boy. And to tell me he plays tuba now, I don't know. He's dead. Since…

881.t: First trombone and lessons from William Robinson, Dutre and Roy
881.s: His first teacher gave him a trombone; he then learned from Dutre and Roy Palmer.
881.ch: Learning trombone and the Wisconsin Roof years
881.q: He was from God? Yeah, you see, I didn't care for the trombone when I did become interested, because I used to whistle a lot of clarinet parts, I'd say. And right up until there I can do that. And so Joe told me, I said, well, you used to get stuff from me. Joe said, partner says, you don't need no…

55.t: Roy Palmer, Fess and Bill's lessons
55.s: Palmer's style, and Bill's own first lessons and teaching Eddie Pearson.
55.q: Palmer? Uh huh. Palmer was in between them. Roy Palmer. He was a good musician. Baratone and trombone. He played at the villa. One place, one spot all the time. Him and the old dude you see the old piano around you, play around you, all that you see. And he was playing there with Fess. Old Fess had…

690.t: Learning trombone then trumpet; teachers; ragtime and marches
690.s: Pope began briefly on trombone, switched to trumpet, took lessons from other teachers, and played ragtime and Sousa marches against visiting bands at Carnival.
690.q: No, I had what you call a vowel trombone. Oh, you did. That was very short, just probably a month or so, you know, I changed to the trumpet.

483.t: Sheik and Howard coming for lessons
483.s: Kelly recalls Sheik and Howard coming to the house for lessons, Chris turning Howard from drums to trumpet, and the easy social life of the neighbourhood.
483.q: Sheik used to come all the time and take lessons. My dad would try to learn different things about, you know, the expression and the feelings of music. You see, you don't just have to know music. Mm-hmm. You know, you have to play what you feel as well. Mm-hmm.

198.t: Teachers and lessons: Picou, Bechet and Barnes
198.s: Barnes says he went to a well-known teacher and to Picou but did not keep up; he and Bechet went to teachers and learned in the district.
198.ch: Zue Robertson, Bakke family and teachers
198.q: No I couldn't answer on that. But I know that… That Shara Nees… Oh yeah. You see he was a teacher for most of the musicians. You see? Yeah I've heard a lot about him. Yeah. Now I don't know if he… he… he… he… teach those or not, but he was well known. All the musicians went to him, because I went…

301.t: Lessons from his father and Professor Mineta's praise
301.s: His father taught him, a lesson dispute ended them; Russell relays Mineta's praise of the father as teacher, and the method book used.
301.q: Professor Mineta, you know, who played with you the other night, claims that he learned all he knows, mostly about clarinet from your father, that he was a wonderful teacher. And he's told us what a wonderful musician he was. Probably so.

58.t: More reading and get-off musicians; an unnamed teacher; tape end
58.s: Miller talks about Kaza and band leaders but cannot recall a teacher's name before the tape runs out.
58.q: But all them boys was out there in the field like me, all them got off, I ain't kidding, every one of them. Every one of them. Now this Louis Demand, he didn't get off, but he always had good music. What about a guy like Kaza? Kaza played with Sackton. Clarinet and Sackton. Clarinet and Sackton,…

574.s: Perkins wrote out scales, charged a dollar a lesson with two lessons a week, and used no method book.
574.q: Yeah, that's right. Yeah, that's was wonderful times then. When I first came down here we used to, when I did start to go in Goodwill, things were pretty good. That's in the 20s, early 20s. Well in 26 I was playing with Chris Keller.

833.t: Humphrey's teaching: his home on Kidders Street, fees and lesson schedule
833.s: Robinson describes where Humphrey taught, how often he went, and what he was charged.
833.ch: Clarinet and lessons with Jim Humphrey
833.q: At his home. At his home. At his home. Grew uptown there. On Kidders Street. Oh, yeah. In Robeson, I think it was. Yeah.

307.t: Lesson price, a strict teacher, and reading the red book
307.s: Lessons cost 25 cents for half an hour weekly; Chaligny slapped wrong notes, played only a poor trumpet, but taught him to read from a red brass band book for about a year.
307.q: Yeah, 25 cents. 25 cents, that's what I was paying. And if I'm not mistaken, it went up just a little bit. Might have only 50 cents after it. That's 25 cents a lesson. Was he a very strict teacher or how did he do? Oh, he was very strict. Yeah.

308.t: Lessons and influence from Cottrell and drum methods
308.s: Living near Cottrell he got pointers and encouragement to read, and a first method book from Doc Souchon's relation.
308.q: Oh, that's around in, let's see, it's 26, 25. It was, it ranged all around, say from 24 all through 26 like that. Oh, man. The old man was playing with P. Ron band. Mm-hmm.

199.s: He took lessons in Hogan's studio on LaSalle Street; Hogan was a gifted teacher and his brother Wilbert played drums.
199.q: I weren't there in the daytime, so I can't say we went on in the day. But at night they had, Professor Hogan, he was teaching, that's how I got to meet him. That's how I got to take private lessons after I left from school, because I used to go to his studio back on LaSalle Street.

997.s: He studied with Cottrell for six or seven months at about eighteen, after already playing in organised groups; Cottrell's later records with Piron are mentioned.
997.q: Well, all I know is he's one of the finest drummers around the city of New Orleans, I can tell you that. That's what everybody said. Played with Excelsior Brass, brass man. Yeah, it was techno. How long did you go to him? All about a few months, six, seven months until he passed.

3.t: Muggsy Spanier learned from Tommy Ladnier
3.s: They agree Muggsy Spanier took lessons from Ladnier at her house every Saturday.
3.q: He taught him. I know he used to come there every Saturday and take his lessons.

129.t: Learning jazz without teachers: Bermuda practice, a fake book, melody playing
129.s: Roy Marsh refused to teach him; he practised daily in Bermuda, learned tunes from a fake book and favours melody.
129.q: Nobody would teach me. The only person that was playing vibes then was a man called Roy Marsh. He was working with one of these big bands. It was Eric Winstone’s big band, and three or four of the guys in the band, they came to the theater to play, and three or four of them came down to hear me…

437.t: Joe Morello around the house and as a taskmaster
437.s: Morello visited his father, tested him on his left hand, and later gave him lessons in New Jersey.
437.ch: Growing up with his father and Joe Morello
437.q: Well he was around the house quite a bit when I was growing up, because he was friends with my dad. And when he was traveling with the quartet he used to come home to his family and inevitably stop by and see my father, and talk about the road and what was going on and give the latest album to my…

157.t: The Dunes show: hardest book and tangents on teachers
157.s: Hal describes the punishing Dunes book shared with Charlie Turner and studying with Grupp and meeting Bob McCoy.

810.t: Making a living and studying with Dave Holland
810.s: Lamb's landlord near Woodstock was Dave Holland, who had Lamb help him recover from heart surgery, changing Lamb's approach to improvising.
810.ch: Learning, living and the Colorado years
810.q: Sure. But never to the point of, you know, red alert. Never to that point. It always worked out. You know like after Rod left and I started the new Dry Jack thing, you know there was some financial struggles but like for instance right after that band broke up I moved into an apartment down near…

338.s: He studied privately with Zimmermann for about seven years; Zimmermann was not a jazz player but supportive, and recommended him for The Bell Telephone Hour.
338.ch: Boston youth and learning the bass
338.q: Well I did jazz playing, not so much with him, no. He had a feel for it. You know he was with the Philharmonic and he taught at Juilliard during that period. He wasn’t a jazz player but he was loose. He was a good golfer, he was a marvelous painter, and he loved the bass, he adored the bass. And he…

523.s: Raph explains that Benny Powell studied bass trombone with him after Lew Van Haney left for Indiana.
523.q: Benny studied with me. Lew Van Haney was the second trombone player with the New York Philharmonic. And Benny and two other guys from the Basie band studied with Lew. And Van Haney moved out to Indiana to take a job teaching there. And I inherited Benny Powell as a student. Benny studied with me…

447.t: Lessons with Kenny Davern: listening and martinis
447.s: Davern never taught jazz directly but showed upper-register fingerings and listened to records with him.
447.q: I mean what he did is kind of steer me in the right direction. As a matter of fact I was with him in Sarasota at the Sarasota festival a couple of weeks ago and we were talking about this, because it was thirty years ago you know, practically thirty years ago. And he says, “The way I remember it is…

470.t: Cello versus trombone and the teachers Teraspulsky and Winold
470.s: Cello did not draw on his trombone hearing, and only strict lessons from Leopold Teraspulsky and Helga Winold fixed his fundamentals.
470.ch: A broken jaw and the switch to cello
470.q: I don’t think that it can be 180 degrees, that big a dichotomy. No, it didn’t help me. It didn’t help me. It turns out that what I play sounds like what I played on trombone, because it’s the same register . . .

686.t: Trombone teachers: symphony players, Slide Hampton, Curtis Fuller
686.s: He studied with local symphony trombonists, then received encouragement and a few harmonic ideas from Slide Hampton and Curtis Fuller.
686.q: I had a number of local teachers, mostly with the symphony. Greg Miller was in – in fact, he’s in the Louisiana Philharmonic still, but he was in the New Orleans Symphony then. And a couple of different guys. The names escape me. But I went to the Eastern Music Festival. I had Gregory Cox. He was…

102.s: A Met Opera first-chair teacher told him to choose between money and learning the trombone, and said they would work on what comes out of the horn. He developed a classical sound.
102.ch: New York scene: Mingus, Flanagan, Moody, Quincy
102.q: Yeah. The sad thing is that when I went to Juilliard, I’m finally in this wonderful school. I have this teacher that is the best and he plays the first chair at the Metropolitan Orchestra. The first lesson he says, “Okay Mac, before we play a not let’s get something straight.” He says, “Do you want…

87.t: Studying with Jaroslav Cimera in Chicago
87.s: After joining Hines he took lessons from the Polish teacher, prompted by Billy Franklin and Louis Taylor, and became his most apt student.
87.ch: Learning the trombone and jam sessions
87.q: In fact I never really took a trombone lesson from a good trombone teacher until I got with Earl Hines. I never did really take an interest in really getting to the foundation, the basics of it. And then once I started it was hard to stop because it was like a new world to me, something I really…

677.t: Private lessons: Doc Hyder, Caruso, Larry Collins and the Arban book
677.s: He took few lessons, then in New York studied breathing with Caruso and Larry Collins and used the standard Arban method.
677.q: Just a few here and there. There was Doc Hyder a few times, and this one and that one. I tried to pick up because I felt that I could -- I only wanted the mechanical structure from teachers. The tone and all of that I would like to create myself, so --

409.t: How the schooling got him the Fletcher Henderson job
409.s: His reading and phrasing training let him play first trumpet with Fletcher Henderson with no rehearsal when Pop Smith quit.
409.q: I'll tell you. By him doing that, I got a break. I got one of the biggest breaks in my life. That's how I became known, by him making me do that. I come to New

28.s: He studied intermittently with Slossberg, teacher of Bunny Berigan, a trumpet virtuoso who adored Armstrong but told him to be himself.
28.ch: Newark and first years in Harlem
28.q: I started to go to school again on the trumpet. I was going to school with a teacher name of Slessberg (PHONETIC). He was a great teacher. He's the one who taught Bunny) Berigan.

641.t: Reading music and what Manuel Roque taught
641.s: Some bands read, Toots did not; Roque taught him waltzes, scales and simple tunes, more than Picou ever did, with Fritz giving free lessons.
641.ch: Clarinet teachers and the Baton Rouge scene
641.q: I had to have a book to start with. He taught me the waltz, and he taught me the scales, and things like that, and the simple tunes to play. In fact, he taught me more than Picou ever taught me. Now, that's the only teacher I ever had in Baton Rouge, was Manuel Roque, and Isadore Fritz(?) would…

387.s: Salary of two or three charts weekly allowed lessons.
387.q: Yes; and that was nice. Because of that I could now take lessons, which is what I wanted to do. There was always something beckoning, something beyond which I had. I still do that. That's part of the Judeo-Christian heritage. That's the way it is; I still keep looking for something that's not…

79.t: Bandmaster Richardson and the St. Louis trumpet studio
79.s: Besides bandmaster Richardson, Thomas studied weekly with St. Louis Symphony trumpeters Gustadt, Carrionie and Olivieri at $3.50 per half hour.
79.ch: Trumpet teachers and St. Louis heroes
79.q: Yeah, I could think of his name. He played trumpet. He wasn't a tremendous trumpet player but he was a tremendous teacher. And during the course of that time they had a trumpet studio in St. Louis. So, I left Mr. Langford and moved up to Jeff City now. And I'm talking to a few people, I heard about…
